claim: Renshaw cells (V1R) are excitable as soon as they reach their final location next to the spinal motoneurons.
source: Renshaw cells (V1R) are excitable as soon as they reach their final location next to the spinal motoneurons and are functionally heterogeneous.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a direct assertion about V1R properties.

claim: Renshaw cells are functionally heterogeneous during early embryonic development.
source: Renshaw cells (V1R) are excitable as soon as they reach their final location next to the spinal motoneurons and are functionally heterogeneous.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing different firing patterns.

claim: Embryonic V1R are subdivided into several functional clusters from E11.5.
source: We found that these interneurons are subdivided into several functional clusters from E11.5 and then display an unexpected transitory involution process during which they lose their ability to sustain tonic firing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cluster analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Embryonic V1R display a transitory involution process during which they lose their ability to sustain tonic firing.
source: We found that these interneurons are subdivided into several functional clusters from E11.5 and then display an unexpected transitory involution process during which they lose their ability to sustain tonic firing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by developmental data in Figure 4.

claim: The ratio of persistent sodium conductance to delayed rectifier potassium conductance controls the diversity of discharge patterns in embryonic V1R.
source: We demonstrated that the essential factor controlling the diversity of the discharge pattern of embryonic V1R is the ratio of a persistent sodium conductance to a delayed rectifier potassium conductance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and modeling in Figure 7.

claim: Emergent neurons begin to synchronize soon after the onset of synapse formation, generating long episodes of low-frequency (<0.01 Hz) correlated spontaneous network activity (SNA).
source: Remarkably, emergent neurons begin to synchronize soon after the onset of synapse formation, generating long episodes of low-frequency (<0.01 Hz) correlated spontaneous network activity (SNA) (O'Donovan, 1999; Saint-Amant, 2010; Blankenship and Feller, 2010; Myers et al., 2005; Milner and Landmesser, 1999; Hanson and Landmesser, 2003; Momose-Sato and Sato, 2013; Khazipov and Luhmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In the mouse embryonic spinal cord, SNA is driven by an excitatory cholinergic-GABAergic loop between motoneurons and interneurons.
source: In the mouse embryonic spinal cord (SC), SNA is driven by an excitatory cholinergic-GABAergic loop between motoneurons (MNs) and interneurons (INs), GABA being depolarizing before embryonic day 16.5 (E16.5) (Allain et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the mechanism.

claim: GABA is depolarizing before embryonic day 16.5 (E16.5) in the mouse embryonic spinal cord.
source: In the mouse embryonic spinal cord (SC), SNA is driven by an excitatory cholinergic-GABAergic loop between motoneurons (MNs) and interneurons (INs), GABA being depolarizing before embryonic day 16.5 (E16.5) (Allain et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: SNA emerges around E12.5 in the mouse embryonic spinal cord.
source: SNA emerges around E12.5 (Myers et al., 2005; Hanson and Landmesser, 2003; Branchereau et al., 2002; Yvert et al., 2004; Czarnecki et al., 2014), at a time when functional neuromuscular junctions are not yet established (Pun et al., 2002), and sensory and supraspinal inputs have not yet reached the spinal motor networks (Angelim et al., 2018; Marmigère and Ernfors, 2007; Ozaki and Snider, 1997; Ballion et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to support the timing.

claim: Functional neuromuscular junctions are not yet established at E12.5 in the mouse embryo.
source: SNA emerges around E12.5 (Myers et al., 2005; Hanson and Landmesser, 2003; Branchereau et al., 2002; Yvert et al., 2004; Czarnecki et al., 2014), at a time when functional neuromuscular junctions are not yet established (Pun et al., 2002), and sensory and supraspinal inputs have not yet reached the spinal motor networks (Angelim et al., 2018; Marmigère and Ernfors, 2007; Ozaki and Snider, 1997; Ballion et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the developmental timing.

claim: Sensory and supraspinal inputs have not yet reached the spinal motor networks at E12.5.
source: SNA emerges around E12.5 (Myers et al., 2005; Hanson and Landmesser, 2003; Branchereau et al., 2002; Yvert et al., 2004; Czarnecki et al., 2014), at a time when functional neuromuscular junctions are not yet established (Pun et al., 2002), and sensory and supraspinal inputs have not yet reached the spinal motor networks (Angelim et al., 2018; Marmigère and Ernfors, 2007; Ozaki and Snider, 1997; Ballion et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to support the developmental timing.

claim: SNA is an essential component in neuronal networks formation.
source: Several studies pointed out that SNA is an essential component in neuronal networks formation (Moody and Bosma, 2005; Spitzer, 2006; Katz and Shatz, 1996; Hanson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: Pharmacologically induced disturbances of SNA between E12.5 and E14.5 induce defects in the formation of motor pools, in motor axon guidance to their target muscles, and in the development of motor networks.
source: In the SC, pharmacologically induced disturbances of SNA between E12.5 and E14.5 induce defects in the formation of motor pools, in motor axon guidance to their target muscles, and in the development of motor networks (Myers et al., 2005; Hanson et al., 2008; Hanson and Landmesser, 2004; Hanson and Landmesser, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to support the functional importance of SNA.

claim: During SNA episodes, long-lasting giant depolarization potentials (GDPs) are evoked in the spinal cord, mainly by the massive release of GABA onto motoneurons.
source: During SNA episodes, long-lasting giant depolarization potentials (GDPs) are evoked in the SC, mainly by the massive release of GABA onto MNs (Czarnecki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the mechanism.

claim: Immature Renshaw cells (V1R) are likely the first GABAergic partners of motoneurons in the mouse embryo.
source: Immature Renshaw cells (V1R) are likely the first GABAergic partners of MNs in the mouse embryo (Benito-Gonzalez and Alvarez, 2012; Boeri et al., 2018), and the massive release of GABA during SNA probably requires that many of them display repetitive action potential (AP) firing or plateau potential (PP) activity (Boeri et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the developmental relationship.

claim: V1R exhibit heterogeneous excitability properties when SNA emerges in the spinal cord.
source: We recently found that V1R exhibit heterogeneous excitability properties when SNA emerges in the SC (Boeri et al., 2018) in contrast to adult Renshaw cells that constitute a functionally homogeneous population (Perry et al., 2015; Bikoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the developmental heterogeneity.

claim: Adult Renshaw cells constitute a functionally homogeneous population.
source: We recently found that V1R exhibit heterogeneous excitability properties when SNA emerges in the SC (Boeri et al., 2018) in contrast to adult Renshaw cells that constitute a functionally homogeneous population (Perry et al., 2015; Bikoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the contrast with embryonic V1R.

claim: At E12.5, V1R display four main firing patterns: single spiking (SS), repetitive spiking (RS), mixed events (ME), and plateau potential (PP).
source: Their response to a 2 s suprathreshold depolarizing current steps revealed four main patterns, depending on the recorded IN (Boeri et al., 2018): (1) single spiking (SS) V1R that fires only 1–3 APs at the onset of the depolarizing pulse, (2) repetitive spiking (RS) V1R, (3) mixed events (ME) V1R that show an alternation of APs and PPs, or (4) V1R that displays a long-lasting sodium-dependent PP (Figure 1A1–A4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A1-A4.

claim: Removing external calcium had no effect on potassium current I/V curves in embryonic V1R at E12.5.
source: Removing external calcium had no effect on potassium current I/V curves (data not shown), suggesting that calcium-dependent potassium currents are not yet present at E12.5.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on experimental observation.

claim: Calcium-dependent potassium currents are not yet present at E12.5 in embryonic V1R.
source: Removing external calcium had no effect on potassium current I/V curves (data not shown), suggesting that calcium-dependent potassium currents are not yet present at E12.5.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of calcium removal on potassium currents.

claim: Increasing 4-AP concentrations from 3 μM to 300 μM changed the firing pattern of SS V1R in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Applying 4-AP at concentrations ranging from 3 μM to 300 μM changed the firing pattern of SS V1R (n = 10; N = 10) in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2A1–A3).
evidence: This is stated in the text with sample size and illustrated in Figure 2A1-A3.

claim: In 50% of SS V1R, increasing 4-AP concentrations transformed SS V1R into PP V1R with the sequence: SS → RS → ME → PP.
source: In 50% of the recorded V1R, increasing 4-AP concentrations successfully transformed SS V1R into PP V1R with the following sequence: SS → RS → ME → PP (Figure 2A1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a specific percentage and illustrated in Figure 2A1.

claim: Application of 300 μM 4-AP on RS V1R at E12.5 evoked mixed events or plateau potentials.
source: Application of 300 μM 4-AP on RS V1R at E12.5 evoked MEs or PPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Plateau potentials and repetitive spiking evoked in the presence of 300 μM 4-AP were fully blocked by 0.5–1 μM TTX.
source: PPs and RS evoked in the presence of 300 μM 4-AP were fully blocked by 0.5–1 μM TTX, indicating that they were generated by voltage-gated Na+ channels (Figure 2B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Application of 300 μM of 4-AP induced a significant 30.5 ± 12.4% increase in input resistance.
source: It should be noted that the application of 300 μM of 4-AP induced a significant 30.5 ± 12.4% increase (p=0.0137; Wilcoxon test) of the input resistance (1.11 ± 0.08 GΩ versus 1.41 ± 0.12 GΩ; n = 11; N = 11).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values, statistical test, and sample size.

claim: Cluster analysis revealed that the most likely number of clusters for V1R at E12.5 is 5.
source: Cluster analysis based on these three parameters showed that the most likely number of clusters was 5 (Figure 3A, B), as determined by the silhouette width measurement (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The cluster with the largest ½Ad (mean ½Ad = 833.5 ± 89.99 ms) and the largest ddr (0.441 ± 0.044) contained all PP V1R (n = 35; N = 29).
source: The cluster with the largest ½Ad (mean ½Ad = 833.5 ± 89.99 ms) and the largest ddr (0.441 ± 0.044) contained all PP V1R (n = 35; N = 29) (Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A2, C2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values and sample sizes, and illustrated in Figures 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A2, C2.

claim: The cluster with the shortest ½Ad (9.73 ± 0.66 ms) and the lowest ddr (0.0051 ± 0.0004) contained all SS V1R (n = 46; N = 37).
source: Similarly, the cluster with the shortest ½Ad (9.73 ± 0.66 ms) and the lowest ddr (0.0051 ± 0.0004) contained all SS V1R (n = 46; N = 37) (Figure 3C, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A2, C2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values and sample sizes, and illustrated in Figures 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A2, C2.

claim: A cluster regrouping all RS V1R (n = 69; N = 61) was characterized by smaller values of ½Ad (23.91 ± 1.43 ms), CV ½Ad (27.36 ± 1.64%), and ddr (0.11 ± 0.01).
source: A first cluster regrouping all RS V1R (n = 69; N = 61) was characterized by smaller values of ½Ad (23.91 ± 1.43 ms), CV ½Ad (27.36 ± 1.64%), and ddr (0.11 ± 0.01) (Figure 3C–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A2, C2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific values and sample sizes, and illustrated in Figures 3C-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A2, C2.

claim: Three embryonic V1R (1.8%) were misclassified in the cluster analysis.
source: It must be noted that three embryonic V1R (1.8%) were apparently misclassified since they were aggregated within the RS cluster although having zero CV ½Ad (Figure 3C, arrows).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a specific percentage and illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: RS neurons represent 41% of V1R at E12.5.
source: However, RS neurons already represent 41% of V1R at E12.5.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the cluster analysis data.

claim: Input capacitance increased significantly at the transition between E13.5 and E15.5 to reach about 23.5 pF at E15.5 in V1R.
source: However, it increased significantly at the transition between the two developmental periods (E13.5–E15.5) to reach about 23.5 pF at E15.5 (Figure 4A1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4A1.

claim: Spike threshold decreased significantly between the first and the second developmental phases, dropping from about –34 mV at E12.5 to about –41 mV at E16.5 in V1R.
source: Spike threshold also decreased significantly between the first and the second developmental phases, dropping from about –34 mV at E12.5 to about –41 mV at E16.5 (Figure 4A3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 4A3.

claim: The developmental transition around E14.5 corresponds to the critical stage at which SNA gives way to a locomotor-like activity.
source: Interestingly, this developmental transition around E14.5 corresponds to the critical stage at which SNA gives way to a locomotor-like activity (Yvert et al., 2004; Allain et al., 2010; Branchereau et al., 2000) and rhythmic activity becomes dominated by glutamate release rather than acetylcholine release (Myers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to support the developmental timing.

claim: Rhythmic activity becomes dominated by glutamate release rather than acetylcholine release around E14.5.
source: Interestingly, this developmental transition around E14.5 corresponds to the critical stage at which SNA gives way to a locomotor-like activity (Yvert et al., 2004; Allain et al., 2010; Branchereau et al., 2000) and rhythmic activity becomes dominated by glutamate release rather than acetylcholine release (Myers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the developmental change.

claim: The percentage of RS V1R strongly increased from E11.5 to E12.5.
source: The distinct firing patterns observed at E12.5 were already present at E11.5 (Figure 4B1, C), but the percentage of RS V1R strongly increased from E11.5 to E12.5, while the percentage of ME V1R decreased significantly (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 4B1 and 4C.

claim: The percentage of ME V1R decreased significantly from E11.5 to E12.5.
source: The distinct firing patterns observed at E12.5 were already present at E11.5 (Figure 4B1, C), but the percentage of RS V1R strongly increased from E11.5 to E12.5, while the percentage of ME V1R decreased significantly (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 4B1 and 4C.

claim: Plateau potentials were no longer observed at E13.5 in V1R.
source: The heterogeneity of V1R firing patterns then substantially diminished. PPs were no longer observed at E13.5 (Figure 4B2, C) and ME V1R disappeared at E14.5 (Figure 4B3, C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 4B2 and 4C.

claim: Mixed event V1R disappeared at E14.5.
source: The heterogeneity of V1R firing patterns then substantially diminished. PPs were no longer observed at E13.5 (Figure 4B2, C) and ME V1R disappeared at E14.5 (Figure 4B3, C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 4B3 and 4C.

claim: The proportion of SS V1R remained high from E13.5 to E15.5 and even slightly increased (91.23% at E14.5 and 93.33% at E15.5).
source: Interestingly, the proportion of SS V1R remained high from E13.5 to E15.5 and even slightly increased (91.23% at E14.5% and 93.33% at E15.5; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific percentages and illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: At E16.5, the percentage of RS V1R increased at the expense of SS V1R (67.86% SS V1R and 32.34% RS V1R).
source: This trend was partially reversed at E16.5 as the percentage of RS V1R increased at the expense of SS V1R (67.86% SS V1R and 32.34% RS V1R; Figure 4B5, C).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific percentages and illustrated in Figures 4B5 and 4C.

claim: No activated caspase3 staining was found in V1R at E14.5.
source: Our data did not reveal any activated caspase3 (aCaspase3) staining in V1R (FoxD3 staining) at E14.5 (n = 10 SCs; N = 10) (Figure 5), in agreement with previous reports showing that developmental cell death of V1R does not occur before birth (Prasad et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with sample size and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Developmental cell death of V1R does not occur before birth.
source: Our data did not reveal any activated caspase3 (aCaspase3) staining in V1R (FoxD3 staining) at E14.5 (n = 10 SCs; N = 10) (Figure 5), in agreement with previous reports showing that developmental cell death of V1R does not occur before birth (Prasad et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Plateau potentials and repetitive spiking recorded in the presence of 4-AP at E14.5 were fully blocked by 0.5–1 μM TTX.
source: PP and RS recorded in the presence of 4-AP at E14.5 were fully blocked by 0.5–1 μM TTX, indicating that they were generated by voltage-gated sodium channels (Figure 6A1, A2), as observed at E12.5.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figures 6A1 and 6A2.

claim: Mixed events, where plateaus and spiking episodes alternate, are observed at the boundary of RS and PP clusters.
source: ME (4.5% of the 163 cells used in the cluster analysis), where plateaus and spiking episodes alternate, are observed at the boundary of RS and PP clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of the data.

claim: Channel noise little alters the dynamics of the model.
source: Altogether, channel noise little alters the dynamics (compare the deterministic voltage traces in Figure 7B and the noisy traces in Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by comparison of Figures 7B and 7D.

claim: Bursting under the form of recurring plateaus separated by brief repolarization episodes was experimentally observed in half of PP V1R (24 out of 46).
source: However, bursting, under the form of recurring plateaus separated by brief repolarization episodes (see a typical trace in Figure 8A, left), was experimentally observed in half of PP V1R (24 out of 46), and plateaus intertwined with spiking episodes were recorded in the 13 cells of the ME cluster (8% of the total sample, see Figure 8A, right, for a typical example).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: Plateaus intertwined with spiking episodes were recorded in the 13 cells of the ME cluster (8% of the total sample).
source: However, bursting, under the form of recurring plateaus separated by brief repolarization episodes (see a typical trace in Figure 8A, left), was experimentally observed in half of PP V1R (24 out of 46), and plateaus intertwined with spiking episodes were recorded in the 13 cells of the ME cluster (8% of the total sample, see Figure 8A, right, for a typical example).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific numbers and illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: The basic model lacks a mechanism for switching between quiescent state and plateau.
source: However, our basic model lacks a mechanism for switching between quiescent state and plateau, even in this case.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a limitation of the basic model.

claim: The mechanism of recurrent plateaus is known as pseudo-plateau or plateau-like bursting (a.k.a. fold-subcritical HB bursting).
source: This mechanism is known as pseudo-plateau or plateau-like bursting (a.k.a. fold-subcritical HB bursting) (Teka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the classification.

claim: V1R constitute a homogeneous population when referring to their transcription factor program during development.
source: V1R constitute a homogeneous population when referring to their transcription factor program during development (Benito-Gonzalez and Alvarez, 2012; Stam et al., 2012), their physiological function (Eccles et al., 1956), and their firing pattern at postnatal stages (Bikoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to support the claim.

claim: V1R constitute a homogeneous population when referring to their physiological function.
source: V1R constitute a homogeneous population when referring to their transcription factor program during development (Benito-Gonzalez and Alvarez, 2012; Stam et al., 2012), their physiological function (Eccles et al., 1956), and their firing pattern at postnatal stages (Bikoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the claim.

claim: V1R constitute a homogeneous population when referring to their firing pattern at postnatal stages.
source: V1R constitute a homogeneous population when referring to their transcription factor program during development (Benito-Gonzalez and Alvarez, 2012; Stam et al., 2012), their physiological function (Eccles et al., 1956), and their firing pattern at postnatal stages (Bikoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings and cluster analysis clearly indicate that distinct functional classes of V1R are transiently present during development at the onset of the SNA (E11.5–E12.5).
source: Surprisingly, our electrophysiological recordings and our cluster analysis clearly indicate that distinct functional classes of V1R are transiently present during development at the onset of the SNA (E11.5–E12.5).
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Five different groups of embryonic V1R were defined using cluster analysis, according to their firing properties.
source: Five different groups of embryonic V1R were defined using cluster analysis, according to their firing properties.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the cluster analysis.

claim: It is generally assumed that, during early development, newborn neurons cannot sustain repetitive firing.
source: It is generally assumed that, during early development, newborn neurons cannot sustain repetitive firing (Pineda and Ribera, 2010; Spitzer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to support the general assumption.

claim: Repetitive firing and plateau potentials dominated at early stages (E11.5–E12.5) in V1R, while single spiking was prevailing only later (E13.5–E16.5).
source: Our results challenge the general view that SS is a more primitive form of excitability (Pineda and Ribera, 2010). Indeed, we show that repetitive firing and PPs dominated at early stages (E11.5–E12.5), while SS was prevailing only later (E13.5–E16.5).
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The transient functional heterogeneity of V1R reflects an early initial developmental stage (E11.5–E13.5) of intrinsic excitability.
source: Accordingly, the transient functional heterogeneity of V1R rather reflects an early initial developmental stage (E11.5–E13.5) of intrinsic excitability.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: A functional involution was described for inner hair cells between E16 and P12.
source: So far, a functional involution was described only for inner hair cells between E16 and P12 (Marcotti et al., 2003a; Marcotti et al., 2003b) and cultured oligodendrocytes (Sontheimer et al., 1989), and it was irreversible.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to support the claim.

claim: A functional involution was described for cultured oligodendrocytes.
source: So far, a functional involution was described only for inner hair cells between E16 and P12 (Marcotti et al., 2003a; Marcotti et al., 2003b) and cultured oligodendrocytes (Sontheimer et al., 1989), and it was irreversible.
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Most V1R cannot sustain tonic firing after E12.5.
source: Because most V1R cannot sustain tonic firing after E12.5, it is likely that their participation to SNA is limited to the developmental period before other GABAergic IN subtypes mature and start to produce GABA and glycine (Allain et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the experimental data.

claim: Embryonic V1R begin to recover their capability to sustain tonic firing when locomotor-like activity emerges.
source: Interestingly, embryonic V1R begin to recover their capability to sustain tonic firing when locomotor-like activity emerges (Myers et al., 2005; Yvert et al., 2004), a few days before they form their recurrent synaptic loop with MNs (around E18.5 in the mouse embryos; Sapir et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to support the developmental timing.

claim: V1R form their recurrent synaptic loop with motoneurons around E18.5 in the mouse embryos.
source: Interestingly, embryonic V1R begin to recover their capability to sustain tonic firing when locomotor-like activity emerges (Myers et al., 2005; Yvert et al., 2004), a few days before they form their recurrent synaptic loop with MNs (around E18.5 in the mouse embryos; Sapir et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the developmental timing.

claim: Low calcium fluctuations within growth cones are required for axon growth while high calcium fluctuations stop axon growth and promote growth cone differentiation.
source: It is indeed known that low calcium fluctuations within growth cones are required for axon growth while high calcium fluctuations stop axon growth and promote growth cone differentiation (Henley and Poo, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the mechanism.

claim: The model provided a mathematical interpretation for the clustering of embryonic V1R shown by the hierarchical analysis.
source: It provided a mathematical interpretation for the clustering of embryonic V1R shown by the hierarchical analysis and accounted for the effect of 4-AP and riluzole (Boeri et al., 2018) on the discharge.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: The model accounted for the effect of 4-AP and riluzole on the discharge of V1R.
source: It provided a mathematical interpretation for the clustering of embryonic V1R shown by the hierarchical analysis and accounted for the effect of 4-AP and riluzole (Boeri et al., 2018) on the discharge.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: Pseudo-plateau bursting has been previously studied in models of endocrine cells and adult neurons.
source: Such bursting scenario has been previously studied in models of endocrine cells (Stern et al., 2008; Tsaneva-Atanasova et al., 2010; Tagliavini et al., 2016) and adult neurons (Oster et al., 2015), but rarely observed in experiments (Chevalier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to support the claim.

claim: Pseudo-plateau bursting has been rarely observed in experiments.
source: Such bursting scenario has been previously studied in models of endocrine cells (Stern et al., 2008; Tsaneva-Atanasova et al., 2010; Tagliavini et al., 2016) and adult neurons (Oster et al., 2015), but rarely observed in experiments (Chevalier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Pseudo-plateau bursting has been observed in the embryonic pre-Bötzinger network.
source: Pseudo-plateau bursting has also been observed in the embryonic pre-Bötzinger network (Chevalier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The interplay between two opposing currents is necessary to explain all the firing patterns of V1R.
source: Our theoretical analysis and experimental data clearly indicate that the interplay between two opposing currents is necessary to explain all the firing patterns of V1R.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the combined experimental and theoretical analysis.

claim: The model can apply to many classes of embryonic cells in mammals at an early stage of their development.
source: This is the case of many classes of embryonic cells in mammals at an early stage of their development.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a generalization of the model.

claim: The wide spread of conductances at E12.5 likely results from the random and uncorrelated expression of sodium and potassium channels from cell to cell at this early stage.
source: This likely results from the random and uncorrelated expression of sodium and potassium channels from cell to cell at this early stage.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an interpretation of the data.

claim: A change in the firing pattern can only occur if a change in inward conductances cannot be counterbalanced by a corresponding change in outward conductances.
source: Our work also clearly indicates that a change in the firing pattern can only occur if a change in inward conductances cannot be counterbalanced by a corresponding change in outward conductances.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the experimental and modeling data.

claim: There is no homeostatic regulation of channel density to ensure the robustness of V1R excitability during its early development.
source: This implies that there is no homeostatic regulation of channel density to ensure the robustness of V1R excitability during its early development, contrarily to the mature CNS (O'Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The poor repertoire of voltage-gated channels at the early developmental stage precludes channel degeneracy.
source: In addition, the poor repertoire of voltage-gated channels at this developmental stage precludes channel degeneracy, which is also known to ensure the robustness of excitability in mature neurons (O'Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: There is no universal pattern of development in embryonic neurons.
source: In conclusion, our study shows that there is no universal pattern of development in embryonic neurons, and it demonstrates that a simple general mechanism involving only two slowly inactivating voltage-gated channels with opposite effects is sufficient to produce a wide variety of firing patterns in immature neurons having a limited repertoire of voltage-gated channels.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a conclusion from the study.
